item.title: Quantum Computing's First Real-world Payoff May Come In Energy Solutions
item.description:
While quantum computing's biggest breakthroughs "are still likely to be years, if not decades, away," CNBC reports the technology is already being tested in energy applications, "from keeping power grids stable to finding better materials for solar cells and hydrogen production." Quantinuum, which was formed by the merger of Cambridge Quantum and Honeywell Quantum Solutions and listed on Nasdaq in June, is using the technology to model materials for hydrogen fuel cells for transportation. It is also working with partners on materials for carbon capture. Another U.K. player, ORCA Computing, a spinout from the University of Oxford, has partnered with BP to better understand how a molecule's physical, chemical and biological properties are governed. That could help explain how biofuels burn and how to make them burn more efficiently... For [quantum software company] Phasecraft, a priority is grid stability and optimization. It has partnered with the National Energy System Operator, the independent system planner that balances energy supply and demand in England, Scotland and Wales, on grid optimization tasks, including managing power exchanges and isolating network sections during emergencies. The company says its software can complete these tasks up to 1,000 times faster than conventional computing... [Phasecraft] is also working with U.K. solar cell maker Oxford PV on the development of new materials for photovoltaic cells capable of operating more efficiently than existing ones. Separately, it has teamed up with London-listed specialty materials developer Johnson Matthey, Harvard University and Boston-based quantum hardware specialist QuEra, in work overseen by the U.S. government's Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E), to discover novel catalysts that would reduce reliance on scarce metals like iridium — which is currently critical in the production of hydrogen. Asked why Phasecraft is focusing on energy rather than sectors that might seem more lucrative, [cofounder/CEO Ashley] Montanaro said the returns were there too. "When you get this right, the commercial returns are real: more efficient energy networks mean lower operating costs and more value from existing infrastructure," he said.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

item.title: GTA 6: 32.5 Million copies, Cameos, and Easter Eggs - but No Physical Discs
item.description:
Grand Theft Auto 6 sold 32.5 million copies before it was even released, reports Yahoo News, which is liveblogging all the videogame history happening after GTA 6's Thursday launch. Like how singer The Weeknd says he found his real-life mansion appearing in the game... How players found a glitch that apparently lets you override the game's third-person point of view to play in first-person. And apparently it's also possible to jack an old woman's mobility scooter. (Though it makes for a very slow getaway, it's reportedly the GTA 6 vehicle that's least likely to crash...) - The jet-skiing dog in 'GTA 6' appears to be based on a real Florida dog. Swim too far out to sea in GTA 6 and a dog in goggles and a life jacket will come to the rescue on a jet ski... Florida locals quickly recognized it. The dog appears to be a nod to Loosy, a golden retriever from Fort Lauderdale who went viral in May riding a jet ski down the New River while her owner, Eddie Inch, towed her along on a jet-powered hoverboard... — GTA 6 isn't approved for sale in mainland China, but that hasn't stopped gamers from getting their hands on it — or Rockstar Games from promoting it there [Reuters reports]. The developer has been pushing the blockbuster game on Douyin, China's version of TikTok, despite the country's strict rules on violent video games. Meanwhile, Business Insider reports that Chinese gamers are circumventing the restrictions by using imported consoles and overseas digital stores. Zac Ling, a project manager at Shanghai-based consultancy Daxue Consulting, said gamers in mainland China could buy 3 million to 5 million copies of the game in its first week. The game's graphic content has also prompted censorship in Japan, according to IGN. - Beloved '80s song parody writer and GTA fan "Weird" Al Yankovic said Thursday that he's the host of the non-stop '80s radio channel Vice City FM in GTA 6. In social media posts, Yankovic said he also wrote some of the in-game commercials and voices the Burger Shot ads. Grand Theft Auto 6 sold 32.5 million copies before it was even released, reports Yahoo News. Cloudflare said PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels, according to the BBC. And "New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access." At its peak, nearly 8 million people were watching GTA 6 livestreams at the same time, Axios reported. PlayStation's network suffered a brief outage Wednesday afternoon as the game became available and players made the required update to their consoles. But since Wednesday evening, it's been smooth sailing. [Around 75% of Grand Theft Auto VI sales have been on PlayStation 5, with the rest on Xbox, the BBC reported, citing estimates from analytics firm Sensor Tower.] Yahoo news shares lots of crazy stories about GTA 6's world-building, like its cameos of real-world celebrities, its in-game hiking trails, and the way a GTA 6 house Rockstar first teased in 2021 hides a conspiracy-minded NPC who's convinced that he's in a video game. But they note that GTA 6 also brings questions on how videogames are sold and accessed: The game is being sold for $80 in boxes containing download codes instead of discs, meaning players can't trade in or resell their copies. "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend," [GameStop CEO Ryan] Cohen told Bloomberg. "Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it's also hurt GameStop." Cohen said the move away from physical games also reduces competition from the secondhand market.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

item.title: Several Waymo Self-Driving Cars Stalled in Traffic as San Francisco's Streets Flooded
item.description:
San Francisco's streets flooded this week after heavy rainfall — confusing several Waymo self-driving cars. The San Francisco blog Sfist describes what happened after the flooding in some places rose as high as three feet: Two lanes of Oak Street by the Golden Gate Park Panhandle were flooded Wednesday morning, with water spouting out of manhole covers, leading to a traffic backup that was made worse by a Waymo that couldn't figure its way out of the situation. The Waymo vehicle came to a stop in front of the spouting water, blocking one of the only passable lanes and worsening the traffic situation, as seen in the video below that is going viral... ["Other drivers had to veer into deeper water to weave around it," reports the San Francisco Chronicle.] Elsewhere in the city, Waymo rider Edward Frazer posted the video below to X, also around 10:20 am, saying that he had been in a Waymo for an hour and a half trying to get from North Beach to Mission Bay, with the vehicle pulling over around 10 times as it encountered flooded streets. The video shows the Waymo on what appears to be Townsend Street near Adobe's headquarters, stalled as water puddles in front of it. Waymo subsequently suspended all service for the rest of the day. But "frozen robotaxis were already clogging San Francisco streets by the time Waymo decided to rein in the fleet," reports the San Francisco Chronicle: Rider Amy Gutierrez said her Waymo suddenly stopped on Fell Street at the intersection of Masonic Avenue, where rain was coursing into rivers. She contacted company support and was transferred to three specialists who tried to move the jammed vehicle. It took a half-hour of false starts before they managed to remotely maneuver it to the right lane. "We were kind of just stuck there — cars were honking," she said, and other drivers were frustrated as traffic backed up. "One person drove by smacking their window, like 'Get out of the way.'" Or, as the New York Post puts it, "Waymos spark terror as they trap drivers in rapidly rising floodwater as monster storm hits California city." Waymos have sparked chaos in San Francisco as they trapped passengers in cars despite rapidly rising floods. Multiple self-driving vehicles were paralyzed across the streets and left those inside frantically calling the company to help get them to safety. One was trapped in the middle of a busy intersection when the car refused to go around an overflowing drain, leaving other drivers to go on the wrong side of the road to get around.... The San Francisco Chronicle also remembers that last year's power blackout caused 1,600 Waymo vehicles to stall "because they required a 'confirmation check' from a human operator before navigating stoplights after the power was cut. Hundreds of requests overwhelmed the system, leaving San Francisco streets full of paralyzed self-driving vehicles." Thanks to Slashdot reader AzWa Snowbird for sharing the news.

item.title: US DOJ Charges Suspected Russian Agent for Stalking Palantir Employees in California
item.description:
America's Justice Department is prosecuting a suspected foreign agent in "a state-sponsored operation" that targeted tech workers in Palo Alto, California. "We will not tolerate any efforts — by foreign governments or otherwise — to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations," said U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian. The alleged Russian agent was arrested in October for "stalking and harassing employees of the software and AI firm Palantir, sources told ABC News, because of its assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia." The indictment says D'iu traveled from Istanbul to Mexico City last June and was connected with a person who helped him illegally cross the southern U.S. border. Once in the U.S., he was instructed to purchase laptops, cellphones and remote access software that his co-conspirators used to help him in his alleged targeting of the company's employees. At one point, prosecutors say D'iu was directed by his co-conspirators to visit a coffee shop where many of the company's employees would work and try to identify them and take pictures of their screens while they were working... In September, prosecutors say D'iu allegedly followed a female employee of the company in his vehicle for nearly 30 miles after she left the company's Palo Alto, California, office. Even as the employee attempted various maneuvers to evade him, D'iu aggressively sought to follow her until she ultimately phoned police and was instructed to drive to the San Francisco Police Department's Mission Station. The nonprofit news site Palo Alto Online notes the government's affidavit "identified at least two other instances in early September in which employees of the defense company reported being followed by a car matching the description of D'iu's silver Lexus SUV. The coffee shops and other locations where D'iu stationed his laptop — sometimes for hours at a time — are in close proximity to the Palantir office in downtown Palo Alto... FBI agents executed a search warrant on Oct. 8 at D'iu's residence in East Palo Alto. There they found the California state ID, passport and Social Security card that were present in the DHL packages, as well as two Russian passports, $18,000 in cash and a notebook with 10 Palo Alto area addresses. Five of them correlate to the home addresses of employees at the unnamed Silicon Valley defense company. The agents also recovered three employee "target package profiles" that included their names, names of relatives, education and employment history, leadership qualities and a list of strengths and weaknesses. After searching D'iu's phone, the FBI found messages from a Telegram contact with photos of four employees and their addresses. D'iu was instructed to act like a food delivery driver and knock on their doors to verify if the employees did live at those addresses, according to the affidavit... If convicted of all charges, D'iu could face a cumulative maximum sentence of 21 years in federal prison and $850,000 in fines.

item.description:

ITV only aired 17 episodes of the original Prisoner back in 1967 and 1968, but it did receive a nomination for Best Dramatic Presentation at the Hugo Awards. Reviews were overwhelmingly positive... The Prisoner, considered one of the greatest sci-fi fantasy TV shows of all time, currently holds a perfect score among critics on Rotten Tomatoes and a 93% with audiences. You can watch all 17 original episodes on YouTube. And apparently the production team for the remake "is apparently full of fans of the initial series," writes Inverse, citing an article from The Hollywood Reporter, "and ITV, the British TV network, is on board as well, which lends a little credence to it." More details on the remake from ScreenRant: Susan Montford, Don Murphy, Philippe Maigret, and Lucienne Papon have signed on as executive producers, but a showrunner has not been selected yet... Murphy has produced every single live-action Transformers movie, as well as the animated flick Transformers One. He also worked with Montford on Real Steel, Shoot 'Em Up, While She Was Out, and Vampire Academy... There have been attempts in the past to create a movie based on The Prisoner, with big names like Christopher Nolan, Ridley Scott, and Simon West all interested at various points, but nothing ever materialized... It took 41 years after the end of The Prisoner for any remake to finally make it to air. The six-episode 2009 miniseries had a solid cast that included Ian McKellen... McKellen and cinematographer Florian Hoffmeister even scored Emmy nominations. Unfortunately, reviews weren't kind to the show, which has a very low 17% critic score and 41% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Thanks to Slashdot reader joshuark for sharing the news.

item.title: Americans Enters Post-Penny World, Businesses Now Allowed to Round Cash Transactions to Nearest Nickel
item.description:
Friday U.S. President Trump "signed the Common Cents Act, which now lets businesses round cash transactions to the nearest nickel, into law," reports CBS News: It sets standards for cash transactions that businesses and consumers can use when exact change isn't available, as the penny is phased out. The legislation calls for cash transactions to be rounded up or down to the nearest 5 cents... Before its passage, businesses could be sued if they failed to give customers exact change, even when rounding up in a patron's favor. CBS includes this quote from an official NACS, an advocacy group for the convenience/fuel retailing industry. "Retailers have been looking for federal guidance on processing cash transactions since penny production ended. NBC News points out that the U.S. Mint said it would still produce collector's versions of pennies in "limited quantities," reporting on what has and hasn't changed now: The penny can still be used as legal tender "for all debts, public charges, taxes, and dues," according to the new law. The Treasury Department said last year that the Federal Reserve will continue to recirculate the approximately 114 billion pennies that are in existence "for as long as possible...." And, as the nickel replaces the penny at the bottom of the U.S. Mint's currency list, that coin can now be manufactured with an inner layer of zinc and an outer layer of nickel [according to the newly-signed law]. It is currently produced with nickel and copper, which costs more than zinc.

item.title: Will AI-Fueled Cyberattacks Lead to Better Funding for Critical Open Source Projects?
item.description:
Remember that famous XKCD comic joking that all modern digital infrastructure rests on "a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003." Politico Europe's cybersecurity reporter wonders if this recent spate of outages suggests that supporting block is coming loose? (Especially after Politico reported Thursday that internal services at EU institutions went offline after a major AI-fueled cyberattack.) Authorities blame the sudden wave of instability on the capacity of new AI tools to detect vulnerabilities in existing code and for bad actors to exploit them... Interviews with more than a dozen cybersecurity leaders and those working on maintaining the internet show the scale of the challenge to keep the web up and running, in a world where the pace of finding vulnerabilities has rapidly and permanently accelerated. Since the web's early days, an unruly cast of idealist engineers and non-profit foundations have been essential for looking after decades-old critical code that's been used to build our digital world. This small army of largely volunteer coders now say they can't keep up with the power and pace of AI. "We're running on fumes," said Robin Bender Ginn, executive director of the OpenJS Foundation, which looks after JavaScript, among the most widely used programming languages. "It keeps me up at night." Cybersecurity agencies around the world rang the alarm last month about major flaws detected in PHP, another critical coding language that underpins 70% of the web. This week, similar scares have spread over Java and NGINX, which also fuel large swathes of technology. Helmut Reisinger, the European chief executive of cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks, said in an interview that the company is seeing "more or less" ten times as many incidents compared to about four months ago. He predicts the constant drumbeat of attacks and scares in the last month is going to become the "new norm...." The rise of AI models and their capabilities of finding software flaws is putting more pressure on open-source software engineers, who are inundated with reports of vulnerabilities — some of which are false or exaggerated. Reports of flaws discovered by AI are "quite verbose," Ginn said. Juhan Lepassaar, the head of EU cyber agency ENISA, said in an interview that the agency has observed a similar pattern of false positives. While some hope the AI-fueled attacks "will put the needs of open source software on the map and prompt an intervention," according to the article, "many of those steeped in the ecosystem... have their doubts." "I'm a bit pessimistic," says Nils Adermann, a PHP Foundation board member. "I worry that people will just not care enough to actually do anything about it."

item.title: Nvidia's Accounting Practices Now Being Investigated by America's SEC
item.description:
We knew America's Securities and Exchange Commission was investigating Nvidia. But Reuters reported Friday that what's being investigated is Nvidia's accounting practices, according to "two people briefed on the matter." Prices of Nvidia shares extended losses and were down about 13% on Friday, according to LSEG data, after Reuters reported details of the SEC probe. They had been down more than 6% before Reuters published its report... The SEC probe is the latest of Nvidia's legal woes. The Justice Department has also been reviewing Nvidia's $12.9-billion deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face alongside a broader antitrust investigation into the company's acquisitions and practices, Reuters reported last month. Reuters says they "could not immediately determine" exactly what potential accounting issues America's SEC is examining." (And Reuters points out that "Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close without resulting in enforcement action.") Their article adds some historical context — that U.S. authorities "have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over possible violations of export controls related to alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China, the US Justice and Commerce departments said this week." And the Financial Times reported Tuesday that Nvidia removed Singapore from its geographical breakdown of revenue sources, Reuters points out, "even as Singapore sales soared to almost half its global revenue." Analysts and investors have also grown increasingly concerned about circular AI financing deals, in which chipmakers including Nvidia have pursued complex financial arrangements to help customers fund purchases of their chips and the construction of costly AI infrastructure, such as data centers... Speaking to Reuters last month, SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock said the agency was examining AI companies' corporate disclosures to ensure issuers are giving investors the full picture on potential risks. On its Tuesday earnings call, Nvidia's interim CEO and former CFO Colette Kress said the company was proud of its role in supporting the AI industry, but would be far more selective moving forward about AI industry financing deals.

item.title: Earth has a New Moon
item.description:
"Earth is currently hosting a second moon," reports CNN: Our planet's gravity captured the tiny asteroid in April. This temporary "mini-moon" — about 2 meters (6 feet) in diameter — will stick around until early December, when it's expected to leave Earth's sphere of influence and continue on a path around the sun. The object is so small and dim in observations that astronomers needed several weeks to confirm it wasn't a defunct satellite or a fragment of one. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center — which tracks asteroids, comets and other small bodies in the solar system — named the newcomer 2026 QQ8 in late October. While mini-moon is not an official designation, astronomers have previously used the moniker to characterize a handful of natural objects, including 2006 RH120, which spent around one year in Earth orbit, and 2020 CD3, which orbited our planet for about three years. However, it's not uncommon for Earth to have one of these transient companions. "On average, there's probably one there at any given time," said Matthew Payne, director of the Minor Planet Center. "They hang around for a few weeks or months. Sometimes it's none, sometimes it's a couple." The catalog of these visitors is relatively short because they usually slip under the radar... The exact origin of the space rock is "an active area of inquiry," Payne said, but most NEOs originate from the asteroid belt, a region between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter that contains millions of rocky objects of varying size that revolve around the sun. Over millions of years, gravitational forces can shift some of these objects' orbits toward the inner solar system.

If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board. The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle's mission was to provide "Universal Access to All Knowledge." Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how "aligned" employees are in their passion for Kahle's goals. "Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle's] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge," Howes tells WIRED. "We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive," [says Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard]. Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive -- which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages -- employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive's building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff's diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, "a unique challenge," but one that's "really rewarding."

item.title: Mercury-Bound X-Ray Telescope Delivers First Images After Eight Years In Space
item.description:
A British-built X-ray telescope aboard the European-Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has captured its first astronomical images after eight years in space and roughly 6.2 billion miles of travel. Phys.org reports: A team led by the University of Leicester has been making calibration measurements with the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), one of the instruments on the two-spacecraft BepiColombo mission to Mercury, which begins its orbital insertion tomorrow (Nov. 21) in preparation for the final stage of arrival at our solar system's smallest planet. After an eight-year journey, it is vital that the team checks how MIXS is performing. Although they have been monitoring the instrument during its trip, it was only in September, following the separation of the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) from the joined science orbiters, Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO) or Mio, that MIXS could finally see into space for the first time and calibration measurements could be made before the orbit insertion sequence begins. The Crab Nebula is 6,500 light-years away and a well-characterized astrophysical source of X-ray light. By observing it, the team can work out the performance characteristics of MIXS in space and compare these with calibration measurements made with the same instrument in the laboratory in 2015. These observations provide MIXS's first view of an astronomical X-ray source. The main observation sequence consisted of 55 spacecraft slews, with 39 hours of observations during Sept. 11-12. Measuring how much the Crab Nebula's image is spread across MIXS's detector helps the scientists measure MIXS's angular resolution, or how sharply it will be able to distinguish features on Mercury's surface. They found this to be slightly better than when it was last measured in the lab in 2015. "During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out," said Professor Emma Bunch, Principal Investigator (PI) for the MIXS instrument and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester. "We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after eight years in space. We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine-tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase."

item.title: Anthropic Mathematician Claims to Prove Riemann Hypothesis
item.description:
Slashdot has been covering the Riemann Hypothesis for years. 2000: Prove The Riemann Hypothesis And Make.Money.Fast 2002: More on Riemann Hypothesis 2008: Claimed Proof of Riemann Hypothesis 2008: Prominent Mathematicians Rebuke Recent Riemann Hypothesis Proof Add a new headline to the list... 2026: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math's great mysteries joshuark shares a report from Scientific American: Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, has claimed to have solved the Riemann Hypothesis with the help of Anthropic's AI model Claude, but the proof is not yet independently verified and remains under scrutiny. [An AI-generated solution of the 167-year-old problem, long considered far out of reach to human mathematicians, would cap off the technology's year-long conquest of math in spectacular fashion.] The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed in 1859 by the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It claims that the locations of the prime numbers along the number line, which appear random at first blush, are actually determined by an intricate, meaningful order. [...] Alpoge posted his Claude proof coded in the programming language Lean, which verifies the mathematical correctness of each argument. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn't take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct. If that happens, it will cap off a year in which AI's mathematical capabilities ascended from unreliable college student to a superhuman force, leaving no part of the discipline undisrupted. [...] Alpoge's statement is elegiac -- recognizing the sense of grief many mathematicians are feeling -- but also optimistic. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light," he wrote, "but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater." [...] The Riemann result, if correct, will echo far beyond mathematics. It doesn't have any immediate real-world applications -- it won't upend global banking or make the internet run faster. But after a year of watching LLMs surpass one math benchmark after another, there is no more staggering achievement it could possibly reach. A machine may have just solved a problem that the smartest people on the planet all agreed they were nowhere close to figuring out. As MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland once put it to me: "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems." "If the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial," says Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile. "Something like a Rosetta Stone." "If true, even from a first high level scan of the summary of the proposed argument, it is very plausible to me that the new ideas in the proof will open up brand new avenues of thinking in number theory and have an immense impact beside the obviously extremely influential result in itself," added mathematician Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and a visiting researcher at Google DeepMind. In a separate article from Scientific American, independent mathematicians say the AI-assisted proof is almost certainly valid. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland said the chance of anything being wrong was "approximately zero" after independently compiling and checking the code. However, researchers are still conducting final checks to ensure the proof accurately represents the original hypothesis and does not exploit any loopholes in Lean's verification system. But did a human beat the AI? The Washington Post reports: Just hours after AlpÃgeâ(TM)s claim circulated on social media, Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society and a professor at Stanford University, said in a hurried statement that mathematician Alessandro Masullo had a proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis without AI several months earlier. The draft, which runs some 940 pages, is in need of significant revisions, Masullo said in a statement, and was not ready for publication. Online observers quickly noted that it contained omissions and apparent errors. But in the introduction to the draft, he published a striking flag. âoeIf any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this,â he wrote. âoeWe are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.â

item.title: FCC Backs AT&T's Plan To Remove Copper Landlines In California
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from PCMag: On Friday, the FCC announced that it was preempting "specific requirements in California law that prevent consumers from transitioning off of unreliable, slow copper lines," even as some residents fear they'll be saddled with spotty cell service as an alternative. AT&T argues that California's "Carrier of the Last Resort" (COLR) rules prevent it from removing the old-school copper network that currently serves only 3% of California households, a number that continues to shrink. In May, the company urged the commission to declare that federal laws preempted California's regulations, thus clearing the way for AT&T to discontinue the service as it prioritizes high-speed fiber and expanded 5G cellular coverage. Friday's FCC order (PDF) partially grants AT&T's petition, agreeing that under federal law it has "explicit jurisdiction over the discontinuance of interstate telecommunications services." Still, the order refrains from "wholly" preempting California's Carrier of the Last Resort rules, and seems to instead focus on the AT&T situation. "While we preempt those requirements that necessitate that AT&T obtain a variety of CPUC [California Public Utilities Commission] approvals before it can discontinue POTS [plain old telephone service] in accordance with federal authorization, we do not preempt the COLR and other obligations more generally," the 74-page document says. [...] Despite the FCC's order, it's not entirely clear if AT&T will pursue the copper landline phase-out in California. In May, the carrier sued to overturn the local regulations and block the CPUC from enforcing them against AT&T, which noted it spends $1 billion each year to maintain the copper network. That court case remains ongoing. [...] According to the regulator, AT&T has proposed discontinuing the legacy telephone service in the state on or after June 1, 2027.

Longtime Slashdot reader fahrbot-bot shares a report from CNBC: President Donald Trump on Friday said U.S. companies will be banned from building data centers in other countries and will face a "tremendous tax" penalty if they do so. "We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference before announcing the new policy -- which apparently came as news to his own staff. "I don't know if that's a breaking story," Trump said. "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now they're here." International expansion represents a growth opportunity for the top cloud infrastructure providers, which want to serve clients from data centers that are nearby, sometimes to meet regulatory requirements. Trump said Friday, however, that if companies want to continue building the centers outside the U.S., "they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them." "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy, and they have everything. They're tremendous assets," Trump said.

item.title: Trump Admin Still Won't Let TP-Link Sell Routers In US
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption. The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security. While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold. Earlier this year, TP-Link announced plans to begin assembling routers in Mississippi as early as 2027, "but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task," reports Ars. "The government reviews of router makers' requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy."

item.title: California Issues Subpoena to Nvidia Over Chip Sales to China

"The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," Bonta said in a press release. "My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information -- and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law." The probe follows Huang's resignation amid allegations involving a suspected Chinese spy and comes as the SEC reportedly conducts a similar investigation. The Hill reports: Bonta's office said the information obtained through the subpoenas will help it to determine if Nvidia, which is based in Santa Clara, Calif., violated state law through its alleged actions. "Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta continued. [...] Following the Huang scandal, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents Thursday showing the U.S. authorized the sale of nearly 900,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips to Defense Department-designated Chinese military companies. An Nvidia spokesperson previously told The Hill, "The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes." item.title: I Don’t Trust Visual Recordings Anymore. But One Day I Will Again
item.description:
In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-old video of what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity.

I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them.

In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be.

The Forensic Approach to Deepfake Detection

Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.”

Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it.

I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.)

I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second.

A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory.Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News

Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters.

My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real.

But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view.

This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake.

Signaling a Video’s Provenance

When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do?

The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording.

Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID, embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin.

Apple recently took these ideas a step further. On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed.

These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be.

Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.”

Real-Time Verification

This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls.

In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again.

All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop.

This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes.

Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today


Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

Unlike the Tomahawk video, which I could sit with for a morning analyzing frame by frame, a live video call offers no time for human analysis. On the other hand, real-time deepfakes pose new challenges for their creators: A fake video call has to be generated at around 24 frames per second to fool the eye into perceiving realistic motion. As a result, the deepfake-video-call software has to take shortcuts, such as simplifying faces and how they interact with their surroundings, and allowing some drift between audio and video or between video frames. The human eye doesn’t notice the shortcuts, but we can forensically expose them.

Provenance signals should eventually play a role here. Video-calling software could apply the same cryptographic signing to each frame of a live video stream that Apple now applies to still photographs. A face swap necessarily occurs between a speaker’s camera and the videoconferencing software, and so the software could verify in real time whether the frames it’s receiving were signed by a physical camera sensor or whether they were altered in transit. As before, the burden shifts from catching the impersonator to allowing real participants to prove they are who they claim to be.

For the first two decades of the digital revolution, forensic analysis—finding the telltale traces of manipulation—was enough to adjudicate most questions of authenticity. The AI revolution, however, has changed the scale and speed of manipulation beyond what forensics alone can handle. To believe a recording is real now, it must also carry a provenance signal from the point of recording. The two approaches work together, with provenance allowing good actors to be trusted, while forensic analyses root out the bad actors.

item.title: Amazon Fights the Delivery Protection Act With Homepage Banner, In-App Pop-Up
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill. When I log into Amazon today, I'm met with a vertical banner that reads: "ATTENTION NYC Council could add up to $5 per order" with a button that says "Act now." The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn't specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I'm logged into Amazon. Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 (518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses. Clicking on "Act now" on Amazon's homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states: "Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we'd no longer be able to work with them, and we'd be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees." The move marks an unusual expansion of Amazon's political advocacy, reports Ars, and raises concerns about the company's ability to influence shoppers and present a one-sided view of legislation. The bill, which also affects companies like FedEx and DoorDash, remains stalled in a City Council committee, with no vote scheduled.

item.description:

All three companies said their core systems or payment networks were unaffected, while JPMorgan emphasized that the incident was unrelated to the banking disruptions earlier this week. Reuters reports: A cyber extortion group called "n0n" claimed on November 16 to have obtained cardmember engagement records that included "hundreds of thousands of campaign interactions for tens of thousands of distinct cardmember email addresses," according to a screenshot of the message captured by cybercrime research platform eCrime.ch. The data includes what appears to be 124 bank employee email addresses and more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some with phone numbers and postal codes, according to a Reuters review. Reuters could not independently verify the authenticity of the data. The same hacking group on November 16 posted similar claims regarding Visa and Mastercard and posted data. [...] The Mastercard data posted by n0n includes marketing data related to customers in North America, the Middle East and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses. item.title: Google Will Launch Android App Verification Requirement Globally In January 2027
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Google announced Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead. It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon. Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven't registered their apps to do so soon. The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google's new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources. Once developer verification is live in your region, you won't be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure. Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps. In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. Apparently, nothing exploded, so the company is now ready to expand. It previously said verification would go global in 2027, and it's not wasting any time with the January start. It says that verification will reach all devices within "several months." So far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with "millions" of non-Play apps already registered. The company says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.

item.title: Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers
item.description:
Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.

Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.

Xue “Alice” Dong


Employer

Colorado State University Extension in Logan County

Title

Extension regional specialist

Member grade

Senior member

Alma maters

Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.

Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.

She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.

“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.

Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).

She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

An early love of design and problem-solving

Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.

As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.

That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.

“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.

She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.

She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.

She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.

That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.

From outreach to extension work

After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.

She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.

She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.

In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.

She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.

Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.

The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.

The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.

Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.

She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.

“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.

Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI. The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly.

How her AI chatbot helps farmers and ranchers

In 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree, in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global.

She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python, a popular programming language. It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it.

The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download.

Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk.

One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch, in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases.

Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication.

Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing.

She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp., Colorado Startup Week, and Boulder Startup Week. And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel.

Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools, she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use.

She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says.

Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.”

How IEEE membership supports her career

Dong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology. She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group.

IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences.

IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.”

She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE.

Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone.

“They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

item.title: Microsoft Testing Remote Lock For Lost Or Stolen Windows Devices
item.description:
joshuark quotes a report from BleepingComputer: Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets enterprise IT administrators remotely lock stolen or lost Windows devices without wiping them. Named Remote Lock, this new feature is shipping to devices upgraded to Windows 11 Insider Preview builds in the Beta (Build 26320.10003) and Experimental (Build 26340.10013) channels. Admins can use Microsoft Intune custom configuration profiles to lock Microsoft Entra-joined, hybrid-joined, or MDM-enrolled devices that run Windows Enterprise, Education, or Pro. After the IT department remotely locks the device, the system can only be unlocked via Intune, since PINs, passwords, local admins, or web sign-ins will no longer work. Microsoft added that the user's credentials will remain valid and can still be used to sign into other devices that haven't been locked. "Windows signs out every active session, hides all sign-in options and shows a locked screen," said Windows Insider communications lead Stephen Lines. "Nothing is erased: the device stays enrolled and managed, BitLocker stays on and user data stays in place. The lock holds across restarts and while offline, and only an admin can lift it remotely, so the user picks up where they left off."
